No. 2026A-623
IN THE
Supreme Court of the United States
_________________________________________________________________________
JESSE GUARDADO,
Petitioner,
v.
STATE OF FLORIDA,
Respondent.
_________________________________________________________________________
On Petition for a Writ of Certiorari to the Supreme Court of Florida
REPLY TO RESPONSE TO
APPLICATION FOR STAY OF EXECUTION
THIS IS A CAPITAL CASE
WITH AN EXECUTION SCHEDULED FOR
THURSDAY, NOVEMBER 5, 2026, AT 6:00 PM
Karin Moore*
*Counsel of Record
Florida Bar Number 351652
Karin.Moore@ccrc-north.org
Capital Collateral Regional Counsel - North
1004 DeSoto Park Drive
Tallahassee, Florida 32301
(850) 487-0922

1
To the Honorable Clarence Thomas, Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of
the United States and Circuit Justice for the Eleventh Circuit:
Respondent’s position that this Court should deny Mr. Guardado a stay of
execution is premised upon mischaracterizations of his claims, the facts supporting
those claims, and misapprehension of the applicable law. Mr. Guardado submits that
he has shown that a stay of execution is appropriate pursuant to this Court’s threefactor test in Barefoot v. Estelle, 463 U.S. 880 (1983).
I. Reasonable probability of certiorari grant
Respondent argues that “[f]our justices would not probably not vote to grant
certiorari on either of Guardado’s questions presented.” Response at 5.
Respondent first argues that Guardado was dilatory in bringing his challenge
to Florida’s clemency scheme so his request for a stay should be denied. Response at
3. Guardado’s clemency process was initiated by the executive branch in March 2026.
Guardado’s interview with investigators was held in July of this year and he was not
informed of the denial until after his death warrant was issued by Governor DeSantis
on October 5, 2026. He challenged it in his successive motion for postconviction relief
seven days later on October 12, 2026. PCR-W 286-307.
Next, Respondent argues that Guardado’s due process challenges to Florida’s
clemency process are speculative. Response at 3. Guardado argued in his petition that
Florida’s clemency process for death-sentenced prisoners does not comply with the
minimum due process requirements under Ohio Adult Parole Auth. v. Woodard, 523
U.S. 272 (1998) because it has not been granted in 43 years, 143 prisoners have been

2
executed since it was last granted, and the current governor’s stated policy that he
will not grant clemency to murderers denies minimal due process and renders the
clemency process a facade.
While acknowledging that Justice O’Connor’s concurring opinion in Woodard
that requires minimum due process in clemency proceedings is controlling,
Respondent argues and the court below found that sufficient due process exists.
Response at 3-5, Florida Supreme Court (FSC) at 10. The lower court also declined to
extend the position held by a majority of states and circuits that those safeguards
must extend to the procedures put in place to implement the clemency process. App.
at 10.
Respondent overlooks that there is a split in circuits and states regarding the
scope of rights under Justice O'Connor's controlling opinion in Woodard. See
Gissendaner v. Comm'r, Ga. Dep't of Corr., 794 F.3d 1327, 1333 (11th Cir. 2015)
(acknowledging split). The majority rule is that the Due Process Clause requires
States to comply with their own State-created clemency procedures in death penalty
cases. See, e.g., Com. v. Michael, 56 A.3d 899, 903 (Pa. 2012); Aruanno v. Corzine, 413
Fed. Appx. 494, 497 (3d Cir. 2011); Baze v. Thompson, 302 S.W.3d 57, 59-60 (Ky.
2010); Young v. Hayes, 218 F.3d 850, 853 (8th Cir. 2000); Sellers v. State, 973 P.2d
894, 896 (Okla. Crim. App. 1999); and Duvall v. Keating, 162 F.3d 1058, 1061 (10th
Cir. 1998). The minority position is that States do not have to comply. Garcia v. Jones,
910 F.3d 188, 191 (5th Cir. 2018); Gissendaner, 794 F.3d at 1333.

3
When the state automatically denies clemency to Guardado and other deathsentenced prisoners, as Florida does, the laws and rules it has put into place to ensure
a meaningful clemency review are defeated and minimal due process is denied.
Based on the foregoing, there is a reasonable probability that four Justices,
when evaluating Mr. Guardado’s claims, will find the issues sufficiently meritorious
to grant certiorari review.
II. Significant possibility of reversal
Respondent argues that there is no significant possibility of reversal on the
issue. Based upon the automatic denial of clemency to death-sentenced prisoners in
Florida that results in the illusory process called clemency in Florida, there is a
significant possibility of reversal.
III. Irreparable injury
The clemency process afforded Guardado and the last 143 citizens executed by
Florida is a facade. If a new clemency review were granted where the executive
actually reviewed the missed mitigation cited in the petition and Guardado’s conduct
in prison for the last 21 years, he would likely be granted clemency. Guardado will
suffer irreparable injury.
IV. Conclusion
Guardado has demonstrated that the questions involving the absence of
minimal due process in Florida’s clemency scheme satisfy this Court’s three-factor
test to grant a stay of execution. See Barefoot, 463 U.S. at 895.
Respectfully submitted,

4
